newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-NZ's Delamere is fiscal conservative.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-NZ's Delamere is fiscal conservative.

text.p: Tuariki John Delamare is the quiet one of the treasury triumvirate.
But he maintains the conservative fiscal line embraced by the National-New Zealand First coalition government since it was formed late in 1996.
Hand-picked by Treasurer Winston Peters as his associate, Delamere must also work hand in glove with National's Finance Minister Bill Birch on the seventh floor of the Beehive.
It is a big leap for the former long-jump champion who went from private life to 17th ranked in cabinet before he had even spoken in parliament.

"I am new to the financial markets and to the non-Maori world, but well-known in Maoridom and in my electorate," Delamere said. He represents Te Tai Rawhiti, one of the five seats set aside for Maori in parliament.

"I think I am financially very conservative. I will not spend a dollar unless I can get a dollar or a dollar twenty cents back. That sort of philosophy pervades both myself, Bill Birch and Winston (Peters)," Delamere told Reuters in an
interview in parliament's lobby.

"So the financial markets can rest assured they know what our monetary or fiscal policy is. It is summed up in $5 billion over three years (the extra spending agreed as part of the coalition agreement). That is the absolute.
"But having said that, and this is a contradiction, there is no such thing as an absolute. We will review things and monitor continuously, but right now we are happy....
"To go rigid and say this is what we decided last year and we are going to stick to it' is irresponsible because conditions change."
His last foray into pure economics was about 20 years ago.

"I had experience as an accountant. I understand numbers, I don't claim to be a brilliant accounting academic, I don't claim to be a brilliant economist, though at least I understand the fundamentals of number crunching."

He was impressed by Labour's finance spokesman Michael Cullen during Labour's failed coalition talks with New Zealand First. Yet Delamere's public criticism of Labour leader Helen Clark for what he saw as breaches of Maori protocol has cooled his dealings with the opposition.

"Cullen is an academic, very bright, has all the theory, but in the end Joe Blow on the street don't read all those theories. I may not be the economic whizz kid that Michael is but I do like to think I have a reasonable grasp of the numbers, of the situation and can survive in the economic debate. But certainly it hasn't been my life."

Delamere may be being too modest. He was present at a crucial meeting with Reserve Bank governor Don Brash during the coalition talks that sealed NZ First's agreement to widen the central bank's inflation target to 0-3 percent while leaving the Reserve Bank Act unchanged.
But Delamere will only say he was there "to provide input ... on the economic and accounting side".
He echoes Peters' tough fiscal line with government departments.

"I was a civil servant ... and I know there is huge wastage. I accept they may well be more efficient than they were in the 70s and the 80s ... but there are massive savings or efficiencies they could make."
"Every dollar every year should be contestable."
He will be in a key position to monitor spending, chairing cabinet's wathdog, the expenditure control and revenue committee.
Delamere is not about to break ranks on the level of the currency -- a key theme of New Zealand First's attacks before the election -- and says the market should set its level.

"We recognise for some quarters the exchange rate is high and makes life very difficult for them -- farmers and exporting manufacturers and the like. But to jump in and artificially try and force the exchange rate -- New Zealand history has shown that if you succeed, the rebound effects are even worse."
He says philosophically he is left-wing on social issues.
"But because by nature I don't like spending a dollar I am probably towards the right on spending. I want all these things. I don't want to spend anything doing them. It is a bit of a contest."
He would like to see regulations on business at a minimum.

"But the late eighties showed that the corporates don't care about anybody else, I don't mean to say all corporates, but there are enough opportunists out there who couldn't give a stuff about anyone and will take the whole country to the cleaners if we give them half a chance."
He does not rule out New Zealand First going into coalition with Labour sometime in the future, but says it will be very difficult given the bad blood between them.
"The absolute bitterness that has come across from several corners of Labour has been an absolute revelation."
"We are more likely to go with Richard," he said, waving his hand at free-market Act leader Richard Prebble who was passing in the lobby.
"The poison that comes over from Labour (during recent debates). It has shown up the real contempt some of those members have for Maori." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
